concepts.name: Speech purpose and audience
concepts.summary: Explain that every talk has a specific purpose (inform, persuade, inspire) and must be shaped around who the listeners are and what they need.

concepts.name: Single core message
concepts.summary: State the one key message you want the audience to remember and understand why limiting the number of main points helps.

concepts.name: Three-part speech structure
concepts.summary: Describe how a speech is organised into an opening, a body and a closing, each with its own job.

concepts.name: Eye contact with audience
concepts.summary: Remember that looking at people in the room rather than at notes, the floor or the screen builds connection and trust.

concepts.name: Nerves as normal
concepts.summary: Explain that nervousness before speaking is common and that physical symptoms like a fast heartbeat are energy, not signs of failure.

concepts.name: Value of rehearsal
concepts.summary: Understand why practising a speech aloud, rather than only reading it silently, improves delivery and timing.

concepts.name: Basic vocal delivery
concepts.summary: Recall that speaking loudly enough, clearly and at a steady pace lets the whole room hear and follow you.

misconceptions.text: Good speakers are born confident and never feel nervous.
Reading the speech word for word from a script is the safest way to deliver it well.
The more points and facts a speech contains, the better it will be.

concepts.name: Speech outline construction
concepts.summary: Build a working outline with a main point hierarchy, supporting evidence and transitions between sections.

concepts.name: Attention-grabbing openings
concepts.summary: Craft an opening using a story, question, striking fact or scenario that earns attention and previews the topic.

concepts.name: Memorable closings
concepts.summary: Write a closing that recaps the core message and ends with a clear final thought or call to action.

concepts.name: Readable slide design
concepts.summary: Apply principles of few words, large fonts, high contrast and one idea per slide to support rather than replace the speaker.

concepts.name: Pacing and pausing
concepts.summary: Control speaking speed and use deliberate pauses to emphasise points and let listeners absorb them.

concepts.name: Purposeful gestures and posture
concepts.summary: Use open posture and natural gestures that reinforce meaning while avoiding distracting habits like pacing or fidgeting.

concepts.name: Timed rehearsal practice
concepts.summary: Rehearse with a timer and adjust content so the talk fits its allotted time.

concepts.name: Basic relaxation techniques
concepts.summary: Use controlled breathing and physical warm-ups to reduce tension before and during a talk.

misconceptions.text: Slides should contain the full text of the talk so the audience can follow along.
Silence during a talk means you have lost your place and should be filled with words like 'um'.
Gestures should be planned and performed identically at set moments.

concepts.name: Audience-tailored message design
concepts.summary: Analyse audience knowledge, attitudes and expectations to select content, depth, examples and tone.

concepts.name: Storytelling for persuasion
concepts.summary: Use stories with a clear arc and relevance to the message to make points emotionally and mentally sticky.

concepts.name: Organisational pattern selection
concepts.summary: Choose among patterns such as chronological, problem-solution, and cause-effect based on purpose and audience.

concepts.name: Voice modulation and projection
concepts.summary: Vary pitch, volume and tempo, and project from the diaphragm, to maintain energy and convey emphasis in different room sizes.

concepts.name: Q&A handling technique
concepts.summary: Listen, restate, answer concisely and redirect hostile, off-topic or unknown questions without losing control.

concepts.name: Slide-speaker integration
concepts.summary: Analyse how each slide's content and timing relate to spoken narration, and cut or restructure what duplicates or distracts.

concepts.name: Feedback-driven rehearsal
concepts.summary: Use video recordings and peer feedback to diagnose delivery weaknesses and target revisions.

concepts.name: Webinar delivery adaptation
concepts.summary: Adjust camera framing, vocal energy, interaction and slide pacing for remote audiences without room cues.

misconceptions.text: A talk that works for one audience will work for any audience if the delivery is good.
In Q&A you must have an answer to every question, and admitting you don't know damages credibility.

concepts.name: Rhetorical appeals balancing
concepts.summary: Analyse how credibility, emotion and logic work together in a speech and balance them for the context.

concepts.name: Reading and adapting to the room
concepts.summary: Interpret audience cues such as attention, confusion and energy and decide how to adjust pace, depth or content on the spot.

concepts.name: Managing difficult audiences
concepts.summary: Judge how to respond to hostility, interruptions and technical failures while protecting the message and the relationship.

concepts.name: Cognitive load in slide design
concepts.summary: Evaluate slide decks against how people process words, visuals and speech simultaneously and revise to reduce overload.

concepts.name: Presence and stage command
concepts.summary: Analyse how movement, positioning, stillness and use of the stage or camera frame signal confidence and direct attention.

concepts.name: Speaking anxiety reframing
concepts.summary: Analyse personal anxiety triggers and apply cognitive reframing, exposure and preparation routines to channel arousal.

concepts.name: Flexible improvised delivery
concepts.summary: Evaluate when to use full notes, key-point cues or no notes and deliver fluidly from structure rather than memorised text.

misconceptions.text: Memorising a speech word for word makes delivery more polished and reduces risk.
Appealing to emotion is manipulative and weakens a rational argument.
Eliminating all nervousness is the goal of managing speaking anxiety.

concepts.name: Original keynote architecture
concepts.summary: Design an original talk with a central idea, emotional arc, recurring motifs and tailored structure for a major event.

concepts.name: Evaluating speeches critically
concepts.summary: Assess speeches by others against purpose, context and rhetorical effect, and justify the judgements with evidence.

concepts.name: Signature speaking style development
concepts.summary: Create a distinctive, authentic delivery style that integrates a speaker's strengths, values and stories.

concepts.name: Ethical persuasion judgement
concepts.summary: Judge when persuasive techniques cross into manipulation or misrepresentation and set principles for honest influence.

concepts.name: Mixed-format event design
concepts.summary: Design talks that engage in-room and remote audiences simultaneously, including interaction, staging and production coordination.

concepts.name: Coaching other speakers
concepts.summary: Create development plans and give targeted feedback that improve another speaker's structure, delivery and confidence.

concepts.name: High-stakes performance strategy
concepts.summary: Evaluate and plan for high-pressure contexts such as investor pitches, crisis briefings and live-broadcast talks, including contingencies.

misconceptions.text: Expert speakers follow one universal formula that can be copied to produce great talks.
Coaching means correcting every flaw so the speaker imitates your own style.
A hybrid event can be run by delivering the in-room talk and simply streaming it.
